title: David-Horodok’s timber trade: making a river town
summary: The river shaped local livelihoods and connected David-Horodok’s merchants and boatmen to wider markets.

editorialConnections.recordTitle: Development of timber commerce in David-Horodok

editorialContent:
## A town at the edge of the forest—and on the water

In David-Horodok, the Horyn was more than a feature of the landscape. It was a route to markets, a workplace, and a force that shaped daily life. The memorial book remembers it as flowing through the town and carrying ships, barges, rafts and steamboats. In the book’s vivid account, timber piled along the shore was loaded onto vessels bound for distant Prussia, while the river’s changing levels could nourish gardens on one bank and damage homes on the other. The [Horyn River](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_9085c65655ce02127c85e577) appears both as an economic artery and as a familiar presence in community memory.

The town’s location helped give that river traffic its meaning. The memorial book places David-Horodok in Polesia, near the Horyn’s meeting with the Pripyat, and describes the Pripyat as connecting Polesia with Volhynia. Those are the book’s own geographical framing and historical interpretation. Independent reference works likewise place the town on the Horyn, a tributary of the Pripyat, and situate it in the broad Polesia region. For a fuller picture of how waterways joined forest districts to markets farther south, the [Pripyat waterway](research:historical navigation and trade on the Pripyat and Horyn rivers) remains a promising line of inquiry. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davyd-Haradok?utm_source=openai))

## Timber becomes a trade

The memorial book’s historical chapter describes a transition in the nineteenth century. After the Napoleonic Wars, it says, economic development picked up across Polesia. Construction and railway building in Ukraine increased demand for timber, which was plentiful in the forests around David-Horodok. In the second half of the century, according to the book, a commercial class emerged around lumber and river transport. Its broad summary calls the merchants and watermen a notable class; its detailed account adds an important qualification: most timber merchants were not wealthy, though together they contributed to a marked expansion of commerce. These are related accounts within the same memorial book, not independent estimates.

The work required practical expertise as well as access to the river. Timber merchants had to judge the quality of raw wood, calculate how it should be worked, and plan how to move it. Watermen—called *berlinshetzkim* in the memorial book—used barges known as *berlinas*. The book contrasts them with the broad, heavy *baidaks* used earlier, which it says had fallen out of use by the mid-nineteenth century. Open barges carried firewood and boards; covered, compartmentalised *berlinas* carried a range of goods and needed crews of as many as eighteen workers plus a captain.

That distinction helps explain the connections among the records. The [David-Horodok timber merchants](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_78d29751189a9b2d0d06cf8d) supplied and prepared forest products; the [watermen](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_172b1668b32eff173b56e0b8) moved cargo between river communities and larger commercial centres. The book does not give a complete roster of merchants, crews or vessels, and its description should not be mistaken for a surviving business ledger. It does, however, preserve the outlines of an interconnected local economy.

## Downstream with wood, upstream with goods

According to the memorial book, spring was the main season for sending firewood and other timber downstream. Barges travelled toward Kyiv and, in later years, Ekaterinoslav; a journey from David-Horodok to Kyiv normally took about two weeks. In summer, crews might haul cargo along the Dnieper. In autumn they loaded food from Ukraine or salt and travelled back upstream, a return journey of roughly forty days. Early winter could leave boats stranded far from home and income.

This was a demanding livelihood: river depth, wind and the timing of the seasons mattered, and watermen could be away for eight or nine months of the year. The [Pripyat River](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_a9063cd086ef31fdbce6a23e) linked those journeys to the wider network described in the book. Recalling the trade, another memorial-book essay speaks of lumber going out and flour returning on rafts, while the river carried goods and news between the town and the world beyond it. These recollections overlap, but they are not identical accounts of every route or cargo.

The trade also involved communities beyond the town. The memorial book describes Jewish families in Nirtcha who dealt in lumber and wooden goods, hauled firewood to Kyiv and supplied food to river workers and travellers. It says the Nirtcha community moved to David-Horodok in 1906, after Duke Radziwill chose the site for a sawmill. The book reports that the mill did not thrive and eventually closed. This story shows that timber commerce rested on a wider network of settlements, workers and landing places—not only on the merchants resident in David-Horodok.

## Vessels, partnerships and limits

The river also carried passengers. The memorial book says that in 1898 five drivers joined to buy a small steamboat, the *Vienna*, which shuttled between David-Horodok and Nirtcha. Its passengers could transfer to larger steamships on the Pinsk–Kyiv route. The book notes that some partners left the venture, and that the remaining owners initially continued to work with horses in winter. Later, another steamboat served Stolin and Gorin, and a partnership with Pinsk Jews established a direct steamboat connection between Pinsk and David-Horodok. Another memorial-book recollection names small boats *Vion* and *Strekaza* on routes to Nirtcha and Vidibor-Stolin. The differing vessel names and descriptions come from distinct passages and should not be forced into one exact fleet list.

The river’s advantages did not remove the town’s vulnerabilities. The memorial book says railways bypassed David-Horodok; the nearest stations were at Lakhva and Stolin, requiring onward travel by road. It also recounts how the postwar border between Poland and Soviet Ukraine narrowed the water routes available to local steamship owners. When the larger Ukrainian connections were cut off, the book says, the remaining routes to Stolin and Pinsk became essential. The [Horyn’s seasonal navigation](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_c4f1fe5492f99caadf8a52e9) depended on shallow water and spring thaw, so river trade was never simply a dependable substitute for rail.

## What independent records add

The Yad Vashem Encyclopedia of the Ghettos offers an independent check on the community’s economic context, though it focuses on the interwar period rather than the nineteenth-century trade. It describes roughly 3,000 Jews—about a third of the town’s population—working in commerce, crafts and industry, including sawmills, other wood-processing businesses and exports of wood products and agricultural produce. This supports the memorial book’s picture of a substantial timber economy while documenting later forms of processing and export. It does not independently verify the book’s detailed nineteenth-century routes, cargoes, vessel names or travel times. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=224))

A YIVO Encyclopedia account of nearby Pinsk provides a useful regional comparison. It describes Pinsk’s position by the Pina and Pripyat, close to extensive forests, and notes Jewish workers’ importance in transport and river trade. That evidence concerns Pinsk, not David-Horodok; it helps place the town’s remembered commerce within a broader Polesian river economy but cannot be treated as confirmation of the local testimony. The Yad Vashem and YIVO records thus add context, while the detailed account of timber merchants and watermen in David-Horodok remains grounded in the memorial book. ([smtp.yivoencyclopedia.org](https://smtp.yivoencyclopedia.org/article/476?utm_source=openai))
